lead: The pipe operator | connects the standard output of one command to the standard input of the next. A filter reads stdin, transforms or selects data, and writes stdout. Chains of small filters turn raw text into answers without temporary files. System administrators use pipelines on log files; analysts use them on CSV exports of sales, UPI transactions or attendance. The same few filters can process a Chennai power-cut log or a cricket score table.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.5 for stdin, stdout and stderr, and Chapter 3.1 for running commands.

blocks.text: The vertical bar | is the pipe operator. It starts the command on its left and the command on its right as two processes. The left command's standard output, file descriptor 1, becomes the right command's standard input, file descriptor 0. Error messages on file descriptor 2 do not enter the pipe unless you redirect them first; see Chapter 3.5.

Write cmd1 | cmd2 | cmd3. Data flows left to right. No temporary file is created. Each stage is a separate process. For example, cut -d, -f1,3 sales.csv | grep '^Delhi' sends only fields 1 and 3 of each comma-separated line to grep, and grep keeps lines that start with Delhi.

A filter reads stdin, does one job, and writes stdout. cut selects fields. sort orders lines. head limits lines. Small filters are easy to test alone and easy to reorder. A pipeline is the whole chain; its result appears on the stdout of the last stage.

cut selects columns. cut -d, -f1,3 uses comma as the delimiter given by -d and prints fields 1 and 3 given by -f. sort orders lines. sort -t, -k2 -n uses comma as field separator, sorts on key field 2 given by -k, and compares numbers because of -n. Without -n, sort uses dictionary order, so 100 comes before 20.

blocks.text: uniq only compares adjacent lines, so sort first. cut -d, -f1 sales.csv | sort | uniq -c counts each city. tee is useful in the middle: cmd | tee saved.txt | next saves the intermediate stream and passes it on. head -n 3 and tail -n 2 use -n for a line count, while wc -c uses -c for a byte count.

A pipeline's exit status is the exit status of its last command. In cut -d, -f1,3 sales.csv | grep '^Delhi' | head -2, suppose grep finds no Delhi line. head still succeeds with status 0, so the pipeline reports success. The failure in the middle is hidden. This is a common pipeline trap.

Bash provides PIPESTATUS, an array with the status of every stage, and set -o pipefail, which makes the pipeline return the rightmost non-zero status. Only a few syllabi teach these. Plain POSIX sh may not have them. For portable scripts, test the important filter separately or write its result to a file.

Each stage is a separate process. A variable changed inside a stage may not be visible in the parent shell. printf 'a\n' | read x; echo "$x" often prints an empty line in POSIX sh because read ran in a process that exited. Use command substitution, a here-document, or a shell that defines the behaviour when the value must survive.
Use pipelines for quick reports on logs, CSV dumps and system output. Test each filter on a small file, then join the stages. See Chapter 3.8 for stricter checking.

spec.aria: Four columns of lines, one per command in the pipeline; struck-out lines are the ones the next command drops, and the last column holds Delhi,120 and Delhi,150.

examples.question: The file sales.csv has five lines with amounts in rupees: Delhi,pen,120, Mumbai,pen,80, Delhi,book,300, Chennai,pen,50, Delhi,book,150. Run cut -d, -f1,3 sales.csv | grep '^Delhi' | sort -t, -k2 -n | head -2. Show the exact output and state the two amounts that reach the output.
steps: cut -d, -f1,3 keeps fields 1 and 3: Delhi,120; Mumbai,80; Delhi,300; Chennai,50; Delhi,150.
grep '^Delhi' keeps lines beginning with Delhi: Delhi,120; Delhi,300; Delhi,150.
sort -t, -k2 -n reads field 2 as a number and orders ascending: Delhi,120; Delhi,150; Delhi,300.
head -2 prints the first two lines: Delhi,120 and Delhi,150.
examples.answer: The pipeline prints Delhi,120 and Delhi,150, so two rows reach the output with amounts 120 and 150 rupees.
examples.check:
rows=['Delhi,pen,120','Mumbai,pen,80','Delhi,book,300','Chennai,pen,50','Delhi,book,150']
c=[r.split(',')[0]+','+r.split(',')[2] for r in rows]
g=[r for r in c if r.startswith('Delhi')]
s=sorted(g,key=lambda r:int(r.split(',')[1]))
print(int(s[0].split(',')[1]))
print(int(s[1].split(',')[1]))

traps: The pipeline exit status is the last command only. head can return 0 after an earlier grep found nothing, so a script may miss a failed filter.
sort -n means numeric sort. head -n 5 means five lines. The letter n has different jobs in different filters.
uniq removes only adjacent duplicate lines. Run sort before uniq when duplicates may be apart.
cut -f expects a delimiter; the default delimiter is a TAB, not a comma. Use -d, for CSV text.
A variable set inside a pipeline stage runs in a separate process. In POSIX sh it may not exist after the pipeline.

quiz.q: What does | do between two commands?
quiz.a: It sends stdout of the left command to stdin of the right command; both run as separate processes.

quiz.q: Why does sort usually come before uniq in a pipeline?
quiz.a: uniq removes only adjacent equal lines; sort brings equal lines together so all duplicates are seen.

quiz.q: A file has lines x:30, y:10, z:20. What does cut -d: -f2 file | sort -n | head -1 print?
quiz.a: cut prints 30, 10, 20; sort -n gives 10, 20, 30; head -1 prints 10.

quiz.q: A pipeline grep Delhi sales.csv | head -1 prints nothing, yet echo $? prints 0. Explain.
quiz.a: The pipeline status is head's status. head succeeded after reading zero lines, so status is 0; grep's no-match status is hidden.

quiz.q: What does tee out.txt do in a pipeline?
quiz.a: It copies stdin to stdout and also writes the same bytes to out.txt, so the pipeline continues.

quiz.q: Why may printf 'a\n' | read x; echo "$x" print an empty line in POSIX sh?
quiz.a: read runs in a separate process created for the pipeline stage; x is set there and does not survive in the parent shell.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production pipelines often chain jq for JSON, awk for fields and xargs for parallel jobs. Named pipes, also called FIFOs, let unrelated processes share a stream through the file system. Search for pipefail, PIPESTATUS, FIFO and back-pressure when you meet long-running data jobs. For kernel details, see Unit 5, Inter-process communication: pipes, sockets and ptrace.
